title: Inside the Beating Heart
summary: Explore the heart’s four chambers and one-way valves, then follow blood through the heart, lungs and body. Watch a heartbeat unfold and finish with a short quiz about how this double-loop pump works.

assets.brief: An anatomically accurate, friendly human heart with a removable front wall exposing four chambers, the septum, four articulated valves and major vessel openings. Use muted red muscle, cream valve leaflets and subtly textured chamber walls. Upright anatomical orientation, apex pointing down toward the person's left; approximately fist-sized, with thicker left ventricular muscle.

A pair of anatomically proportioned human lungs with a central trachea, branching main bronchi and short pulmonary vessel connections. The right lung has three lobes; the left has two and a cardiac notch. Soft pink, lightly mottled surfaces and pale airway cartilage; clean educational style. Upright anatomical orientation, roughly 25 centimetres tall.

steps.text: Your heart is a muscular pump between your lungs, slightly to your left. Roughly the size of your fist, it moves blood carrying oxygen and nutrients day and night.
This cutaway is enlarged, not life-sized. Imagine a person facing you: their right is on your left. The open front lets us see inside.
Four chambers: the right atrium and left atrium receive returning blood. Below, the right ventricle and left ventricle pump blood out.
The septum is a muscular dividing wall. In a healthy heart, it keeps oxygen-poor blood on the right from mixing directly with oxygen-rich blood on the left.
The right ventricle pumps to nearby lungs. The left ventricle pumps around the body; its thicker wall makes greater pressure. The bars compare thickness, not scale.
Four valves guide one-way flow. Tricuspid and mitral valves sit between atria and ventricles. Pulmonary and aortic valves guard the ventricular exits.
In this simplified valve, muscle pressure pushes blood forward. Flaps open, then close against reverse pressure. Valves guide flow; they do not pull blood.

sfx.prompt: Single muffled heartbeat, low lub followed by softer dub

nodes.label: Blue: less oxygen | Red: more oxygen

steps.text: Follow dots representing blood. Blue means less oxygen; red means more. Real blood is always red. Sizes and distances are simplified, not to scale.
Body cells have used some oxygen. Blood returns through large veins called the venae cavae, entering the right atrium, an upper heart chamber.
Blood crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Its squeeze sends blood through the pulmonary valve and pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

sfx.prompt: Single muffled heartbeat, low lub followed by softer dub

steps.text: In the lungs, oxygen crosses from air sacs into blood. Carbon dioxide crosses into air to be breathed out. Only now do our blood dots turn red.
Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium. It crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, returning to the heart before the body.
The left ventricle pumps through the aortic valve into the aorta. In body capillaries, oxygen and nutrients reach cells; wastes enter blood.

sfx.prompt: Single muffled heartbeat, low lub followed by softer dub

steps.text: Veins return blood to the right heart. Two connected loops repeat: heart to lungs to heart, and heart to body to heart. Both sides work together.
Arteries carry blood away; veins carry it toward the heart. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood; pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.

nodes.label: Valve markers: bright = closed, dim = open
Yellow dots represent an electrical signal
Natural pacemaker in the right atrium
Electrical signal to the right ventricle
Electrical signal to the left ventricle

steps.text: A heartbeat is one repeating cycle of squeezing and relaxing. Both sides work together, without waiting for blood's whole trip. This diagram is not to scale.
During relaxation, returning blood fills the atria and flows through open tricuspid and mitral valves into the ventricles. Both atria squeeze to finish filling.
Both ventricles contract. Pressure closes the tricuspid and mitral valves. Higher pressure opens the pulmonary and aortic valves, sending blood to lungs and body.
The ventricles relax. Pulmonary and aortic valves close, stopping backflow. When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, inlet valves reopen.
Lub comes mainly from vibrations as tricuspid and mitral valves close. Dub follows pulmonary and aortic valve closure. These sounds are not valves opening.

sfx.prompt: Single muffled heartbeat, low lub followed by softer dub

steps.text: A natural pacemaker in the right atrium starts an electrical signal. It spreads through the atria, pauses briefly, then activates the ventricles in order.
During exercise, your heart usually beats faster to meet your muscles' greater oxygen needs. More frequent beats help keep both blood loops moving.
Recall the route: body, right heart, lungs, left heart, body. Lungs add oxygen; valves stop backflow. Which chamber pumps blood to the body? Take a moment to answer.

quiz.question: Which chamber pumps blood to the body?

correct.text: Correct! The left ventricle pumps blood through the aortic valve toward the body.

wrong.text: Not quite. The right ventricle pumps toward the lungs, while the atria fill the ventricles. Try again.
